hook.text: In May 2022, Acme Corp, customer forty-two, placed a twelve hundred dollar order from the East. The next summer, it moved West. Today, which region does that order belong to?

hook-both.text: Both answers can be right: the East, as it was, or the West, as it is. What the warehouse says depends on how the customer's row took the move.

plan.text: That row is a slowly changing dimension, or SCD. Nine questions on dimensions that change, and on data that arrives late: seven worked through, then two quick ones.

t1.text: Question one. What is SCD Type one, and when should you use it? Type one overwrites. Acme's region becomes West, there's still one row, and no trace of the East.

t1-history.text: So the past moves with it. The 2022 order now reports as West. Overwrite every customer that way, and every region's 2022 revenue changes. East loses twelve hundred dollars, in a report that already went out.

t1-when.text: Use it when the old value was never true, like a typo in a name, or when the business only ever asks about now. In practice it's a merge on the natural key: update the row if it's there, insert it if not.

t1-mix.text: And types are chosen per column. A dimension that versions the region can still treat the name as Type one, so a fixed misspelling is fixed on every version.

t2.text: Question two. What is SCD Type two, and how is it implemented? Add a row instead. Each version gets its own surrogate key, a valid from, a valid to, and an is current flag.

t2-rows.text: Acme's East row closes on June fourteenth, 2023. The West row opens the next day, valid until a date far in the future. That date, rather than a null, lets one between test cover every version, closed or current.

t2-join.text: Join each order to the version whose window holds its date, and the 2022 order lands in the East, the 2024 order in the West.

t2-load.text: Each change is two statements, run together: close the current row, its end date the day before the move, then insert the new version.

t2-trap.text: The trap is joining on the customer ID alone. Each order repeats once per version of its customer: twenty-four rows become forty-four, revenue grows by three quarters, and nothing errors. Store the surrogate key on the fact at load time, and that join needs no date at all.

t2-current.text: So every query has to say which version it means: is current for today, the window for a point in time. And the table grows with every change, for as long as the warehouse runs.

t3.text: Question three. What is SCD Type three, and what is its main limitation? It adds a column for the previous value. Acme's row now reads West, with a previous region of East.

t3-use.text: That suits one change everybody wants to compare across, like sales territories redrawn: report this year under the old regions and the new, with no history join.

t3-limit.text: The limit is one step. Move Acme again, to the North, and the previous region becomes West. The East is gone, and a third column would only push the problem back a step.

snap.text: Question four. What is dbt snapshot, and what SCD type does it implement? Type two. On each run of dbt, the tool that builds these models, a snapshot compares the source with what it recorded, and for every changed row it closes the old version and inserts a new one, stamped with dbt valid from and dbt valid to.

snap-strategy.text: The timestamp strategy trusts an updated at column. The check strategy compares the columns you list, for sources with no timestamp to trust.

snap-gap.text: Either way, it only sees what's there when it runs. Change a row twice between runs, and the middle value is never recorded.

snap-keep.text: And the source keeps only the present, so the snapshot is the only copy of that history. It can't be rebuilt from the source, so protect it like source data.

snap-model.text: Downstream, the dimension model reads the snapshot, and its two timestamps become each version's window.

late.text: Question five. How do you handle late-arriving dimension records? Here an order for customer seventy-seven lands before customer seventy-seven does.

late-drop.text: Look up its key with an inner join, and the order vanishes: seven hundred dollars loaded, out of eleven hundred ten, and no error.

late-fix.text: Never drop the fact; the sale happened. Load it against an unknown member, key minus one, and keep the customer's own ID on the row.

late-correct.text: When seventy-seven arrives, a correction job re-keys those rows, and the four hundred ten dollars moves from unknown to the South. The other way is to hold the facts back until the customer lands: totals arrive later, but never short.

late-watch.text: Either way, count the rows still waiting. A count that keeps growing means a feed is broken, not late.

late-fact.text: Question six. How do you handle late-arriving facts? Load them at their own event time. Say Acme's 2022 order only reaches the warehouse today.

late-fact-trap.text: Look up the customer's current row, and the order gets ten oh two: the West, a region Acme hadn't moved to yet. Look up the version valid on the order date, and it gets ten oh one, the East.

late-fact-load.text: And make sure it's picked up at all. A load that only takes recent order dates skips it, so select new rows by when they arrived, not when they happened.

late-fact-snap.text: Then rebuild any periodic snapshot for the period the order lands in. An accumulating snapshot just updates its row in place.

measure.text: Question seven. How do you handle a slowly changing measure in a fact table? A measure is fixed when the event happens. This order was booked at nine hundred dollars in March. In April, it turns out it was eight hundred.

measure-reverse.text: Don't update it in place. Insert a reversing row, minus nine hundred, and the corrected eight hundred. Today's total is eight hundred.

measure-why.text: And March's report, run again, still says nine hundred, as it did when it was published. Overwrite the row instead, and last month's number changes under everyone who quoted it.

measure-restate.text: When the rules change, like revenue recognized a new way, version the fact, or keep the restated amount in a column of its own.

r-t0.text: Question eight. What is SCD Type zero? A value that never changes once written, like a date of birth, or the channel a customer first came through. Load it once, and ignore whatever later loads say, even when the same row versions its region as Type two.

r-mini.text: Question nine. What is a mini-dimension? Fast-changing attributes, like age band and income band, moved out of a big customer dimension into a small table of every combination, twenty rows here, with its own key on the fact. The customer dimension stops adding a version every time a band changes, and each order still records the bands that were true when it was placed.

next.text: Every table here is rebuilt each day, in order: the snapshot first, then the dimensions, then the facts that look them up. Running that order is dbt's job. Next: how dbt builds a project.
